D019_m001.question:
It’s been about a week since the accident, and I just don’t feel like myself. I was driving home from school when that truck ran the red light and slammed into the car in front of me. I wasn’t physically hurt, but I can’t get it out of my head.

At night, I lie in bed for what feels like hours, staring at the ceiling. I’m exhausted, but as soon as I close my eyes I see the crash again—the sound of metal, the glass, people shouting. I end up getting maybe a couple of hours of broken sleep.

What scares me most are these moments where I kind of “leave” the room. The other day in class, a book dropped and for a few seconds I was back at the intersection. I could smell the smoke, hear the sirens. The students had to get my attention; I didn’t even realize I’d stopped mid-sentence.

Since this started, I’ve been snapping at my wife, avoiding driving certain routes, and I’m struggling to focus on lesson plans or grading. It’s really messing with my work and home life.
D019_m001.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D019_m002.question:

I work in admissions, so this is normally a busy but structured time of year—emails, campus tours, meetings with anxious parents. I’ll be in a meeting with a student and suddenly I’m replaying the crash instead of listening to what they’re saying.

I’ve started avoiding driving that route to campus, even if it means being late. My wife says I’m jumpy and distracted at home. I’m making mistakes at work, missing deadlines, and I kind of dread going in now because I’m afraid I’ll space out at the wrong moment and screw something up.
D019_m002.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D019_m003.question:

I’ll be fine during the day at the station, running drills, cleaning gear, joking with the guys, and then something small sets me off—like the smell of smoke from a grill—and I’m right back there. Heart pounding, palms sweating, like it’s happening again.

Nights are the worst. I just lie there, staring at the ceiling for hours. My wife falls asleep next to me and I’m trying to shut my brain off, but as soon as I close my eyes it’s replaying—sirens, screams, the moment we realized we were too late. When I do finally drift off, I get these nightmares where I’m back in the fire, or I’m the one trapped, or it’s my own house burning. I wake up soaked in sweat, breathing hard.

I’m snapping at my wife over nothing, zoning out at work. I’m scared I’m not as sharp on calls, and in my job that can get someone hurt.
D019_m003.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D019_m004.question:
